procedural_history.originating_court: Police Station Pimpri, Chinchwad (where FIR No. 806 of 2019 was lodged)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 16.11.2021 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Writ Petition No. 4134 of 2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay quashed FIR No 806 of 2019 in Writ Petition No. 4134 of 2019. The FIR was lodged by the appellant for offenses punishable under Sections 420, 406, 409, 465, 467, 468 and 471 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Dhanraj N Asawani, approached the Supreme Court by way of a Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No 2246 of 2022, which was converted to Criminal Appeal No. 2093 of 2023. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and order of the High Court, thereby reinstating FIR No 806 of 2019.

directions: The impugned judgment and order of the High Court dated 16 November 2021, which quashed FIR No 806 of 2019 dated 19 July 2019, is set aside.
The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of s.81(5B) of Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960 can be construed as preventing a share holder of the society such as the appellant, who was also an erstwhile director, from independently setting the criminal law in motion.

facts: An appellant, who was a shareholder and former director of a co-operative society, registered an FIR against the society's management for offenses including cheating and misappropriation of funds.
The High Court quashed this FIR.

The High Court's reasoning was that the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, is a special law, and Section 81(5B) of this Act provides a specific procedure for reporting financial irregularities (i.e., by the auditor or Registrar), which would preclude a shareholder from filing an FIR under general criminal law.
law: Section 81(5B) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, casts a positive obligation and a public duty on the auditor or the Registrar to file an FIR when they discover financial irregularities in a co-operative society.
A statute can only prevent the application of general law either expressly or by necessary implication.
To determine if there is an exclusion by necessary implication, the court must look at the language and intent of the statute.
The text of Section 81(5B) does not contain any negative language or express prohibition that would bar persons other than the auditor or Registrar from filing an FIR.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's interpretation, stating that neither an express provision nor a necessary implication in the 1960 Act prevents a shareholder from setting the criminal law in motion.

The Court reasoned that the purpose of Section 81(5B) is to ensure accountability and vigilance from the auditor and Registrar, who are often the first to learn of such issues. It imposes a duty on them to act, but it does not create an exclusive right or a monopoly on reporting crime.

The Court found that interpreting the section as a bar would be against the interests of the society, as it is beneficial for financial irregularities to be reported to the police by anyone who becomes aware of them.

Since the provision lacks any prohibitive language, the Court concluded it would be contrary to the basic principles of statutory construction to infer that it debars a shareholder from filing an FIR.
Once an FIR is filed, the police have a duty to investigate, and this process cannot be stopped by citing the duty that Section 81(5B) places on the auditor or Registrar.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's view and held that Section 81(5B) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, does not prevent a shareholder or any other person from independently filing an FIR to set the criminal law in motion. The provision merely imposes a duty on the auditor/Registrar to file a report but does not bar others from doing so. Consequently, the High Court's order quashing the FIR was set aside.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Absent a specific bar or exception contained in a statutory provision, any individual can set the criminal law into motion, as the right to initiate proceedings cannot be limited by the concept of locus standi, which is generally unknown to criminal jurisprudence.
obiter: An offense is not merely a wrong against the person who suffers harm but is also an offense against society, which has an interest in the punishment of the offender for its orderly and peaceful development.
Prosecution for serious offenses is undertaken in the name of the State to exclude any element of private vendetta or vengeance.
A statutory provision is considered mandatory if it begins with an overriding clause or uses negative wording like 'No'.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that Section 81(5B) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, which casts a positive obligation on an auditor or Registrar to file an FIR upon discovering financial irregularities, does not prevent any other person, such as a shareholder, from independently setting the criminal law in motion. A plain reading of the provision does not indicate a legislative intent to debar anyone other than the specified officials from registering an FIR. The police have an independent power and duty under the Code of Criminal Procedure to investigate an offense, and this power is not curtailed by the 1960 Act as there is no express bar, nor can a bar be inferred by necessary implication.
legal_tests_applied: The general principle that absent a specific bar or exception in a statute, the criminal law can be set into motion by any individual.

The principle that the concept of locus standi of the complainant is not recognized in criminal jurisprudence, except in situations where the statute creating an offense provides for the eligibility of the complainant.
The test of whether a statutory provision creates a bar by 'necessary implication', which is inferred from the language and the intent of the statute.
policy_considerations: An offense is not merely an offense committed against the person who suffers harm but is also an offense against society, which has an interest in the punishment of the offender for its orderly and peaceful development.

The right to initiate criminal proceedings cannot be whittled down, circumscribed, or fettered by putting it into a strait-jacket formula of locus standi, as the punishment of the offender is in the interest of society.

The interests of the society will be safeguarded if financial irregularities in co-operative banks are reported to the police, who can subsequently take effective actions to investigate crimes and protect the commercial interests of the members of the society.
